arXiv:2608.21748v1 [cs.CV] 22 Aug 2026

Calibrate What You SHIP:
Post-Selection Risk Control for Verifier-Guided Text-to-Image Generation

Xuanhua Yin, Shunqi Mao, Wei Guo, Chuanzhi Xu, Weidong Cai\corresponding
Abstract

Verifier-guided text-to-image systems increasingly use test-time search to select, refine, or stop among multiple candidates, yet release thresholds are often calibrated on individual images. This creates a candidate-to-policy calibration mismatch: search changes both which prompts receive an output and which candidate is released, so candidate-level risk control need not imply control of released-output risk. We formalize this estimand shift through prompt reweighting and within-prompt selection, and introduce SHIP, Selection-aware Held-out calibration of Inference Policies. SHIP runs or replays the complete deployed policy on held-out prompts, evaluates the image it actually releases using an independent target judge, and selects the most permissive threshold whose risk upper bound satisfies a prescribed budget. For replayable policies with a prespecified threshold grid, simultaneous confidence control provides finite-sample validity. Experiments across fixed, sequential, and adaptive T2I inference procedures show that policy-level calibration recovers lower-risk operating points while exposing policy-dependent tradeoffs among risk, coverage, and compute. On GenEval2 with FLUX at N=16N=16, a pooled-candidate threshold yields released risk 0.3100.310, whereas SHIP reduces it to 0.1620.162. Across 200 cached-stream splits, the fixed-grid certificate has no target crossing. Reliable inference-time scaling therefore requires calibrating the output distribution induced by the complete deployed policy.

1 Introduction

Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems increasingly allocate test-time compute to search over multiple generation paths rather than returning a single independently sampled image. Depending on the inference procedure, the system may explore different noise seeds, rank partially denoised drafts, rewrite prompts, refine unmet requirements, edit intermediate images, stop early, or abstain (32; 25; 29; 48; 10; 19; 23; 35; 34). Fine-grained vision-language evaluators guide these decisions by assessing object counts, attributes, spatial relations, and actions (21; 12; 30; 42; 24). Consequently, the image delivered to the user is jointly determined by generation, verification, search, and stopping. Reliability should therefore be evaluated on the outputs released by the complete inference procedure, rather than on independently generated candidates.

A common approach to improving reliability is to calibrate a verifier threshold on held-out candidate images and release only candidates that pass this threshold (2). Such calibration controls the expected loss of an individual candidate conditioned on passing. In deployment, however, the system does not release a generic passing candidate. It releases the image returned by the complete search, selection, and stopping procedure. Because this procedure changes the distribution of released images, controlling candidate-level risk does not in general guarantee control of the risk of the deployed inference policy. We refer to this discrepancy as the candidate-to-policy calibration mismatch.

Search creates this mismatch through two distinct mechanisms. First, it changes which prompts receive an output. Under sequential stopping, for example, a prompt is accepted if any attempt passes, so prompts with different candidate-level pass probabilities have different probabilities of appearing among the released outputs. Second, search changes which image is released for each accepted prompt. Best-of-NN selection, first-hit stopping, tournaments, rewriting, and refinement select or modify candidates according to an imperfect online verifier (17; 14), so the released image need not follow the same conditional loss distribution as a generic passing candidate. Search therefore changes both the distribution of prompts represented among released outputs and the conditional distribution of the image released for each prompt.

To this end, we introduce SHIP, Selection-aware Held-out calibration of Inference Policies. SHIP runs or replays the complete policy on held-out prompts, evaluates the output it actually releases using an independent target judge, and selects the most permissive threshold whose upper confidence bound satisfies a prescribed risk budget. Threshold-independent candidate streams support efficient replay, while history-dependent search is evaluated through complete policy trajectories. For prespecified threshold grids, simultaneous confidence bounds provide finite-sample control for replayable policies (1).

Figure 1 illustrates how verifier-guided search may prefer an output that still violates the prompt, whereas SHIP calibrates the final release decision under a target risk budget. We evaluate SHIP across fixed, sequential, and adaptive T2I inference procedures, including tournament selection, refinement, prompt rewriting, trajectory selection, and image editing. The results recover feasible released-output operating points and reveal policy-dependent tradeoffs among risk, coverage, and inference cost. More broadly, search determines the attainable performance frontier, while calibration determines which points on that frontier can be released under a risk constraint. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We characterize a T2I-specific candidate-to-policy calibration mismatch, decompose it into prompt reweighting and within-prompt selection, and show that candidate-level risk control need not control released-output risk.

  • •

    We introduce SHIP, which calibrates complete release policies on held-out prompts and selects the most permissive threshold satisfying a prescribed released-output risk budget.

  • •

    We validate SHIP across fixed, sequential, and adaptive T2I search policies, multiple models and benchmarks, and human evaluation, revealing policy-dependent tradeoffs among risk, coverage, and inference cost.

2 Related Work

Text-to-Image Generation and Verification.

Modern T2I systems span diffusion and flow-based generators, including SDXL, Stable Diffusion 3, and FLUX (36; 33; 16; 31; 9). Their prompt following is increasingly assessed through fine-grained question answering, as in TIFA, DSG, VQAScore, Gecko, and GenEval2 (21; 12; 30; 42; 24), or through learned reward models such as ImageReward, PickScore, and CycleReward (43; 26; 3). These evaluators provide useful candidate-ranking signals, but do not by themselves characterize the loss of the image released after search. SHIP therefore treats the verifier as an interchangeable selector and evaluates policy outputs with a held-out target judge.

Verifier-Guided Inference-Time Scaling.

Inference-time scaling searches seeds or trajectories, revises prompts, and edits images using verifier feedback (32; 25; 29; 48; 10). Recent adaptive policies include RAISE refinement, ProbeSelect trajectory pruning, Flash-BoN draft tournaments, and ADE-CoT image editing (23; 19; 35; 34). These methods improve how candidates are produced or selected. SHIP addresses the complementary reliability question of whether the output released by the resulting policy satisfies a target risk budget. We test this composition across fixed search, sequential stopping, refinement, rewriting, early trajectory selection, and editing. Because verifier bias and self-consistency can distort selection (46; 39), our protocol separates the online selector from the offline target judge.

Selective Risk Control for Deployed Policies.

Conformal prediction and its risk-controlling extensions calibrate decisions on exchangeable data (38; 7; 1; 2), while selective classification trades coverage for conditional accuracy through abstention (13; 15; 18). Recent work extends these ideas to bounded selective risks and generated outputs (44; 6; 45; 27; 40). TRON jointly controls sampling and filtering risks for multimodal response sets, but its output is a set rather than one image selected by a release policy (41). Most closely, BOKBO calibrates execute-or-abstain decisions for verifier-best KK-sample vision-language-action policies (37). We therefore do not claim policy-level calibration or its confidence bounds as new. Our contribution is the T2I-specific estimand analysis, its prompt-reweighting and within-prompt decomposition, and evidence across first-hit release, best-of-NN, and history-dependent policies with continuous released-output loss.

3 Method

3.1 Overview and Setting

Let p∼𝒫p\sim\mathcal{P} be a deployment prompt and let ω\omega collect the internal randomness of generation and search. A thresholded release policy πτ​(p,ω)\pi_{\tau}(p,\omega) executes its complete inference procedure and returns either an image or the abstention symbol ⊥\bot, where τ∈𝒯⊂[0,1]\tau\in\mathcal{T}\subset[0,1] is a selector-risk threshold. Its trajectory may contain sampled images, partially denoised drafts, verifier feedback, rewritten prompts, or intermediate edits. Every completed image YY has an online selector risk s⁡(Y,p)∈[0,1]s(Y,p)\in[0,1] and a held-out target loss ℓ⁡(Y,p)∈[0,1]\ell(Y,p)\in[0,1], where lower values are better and the policy never observes ℓ\ell.

We write Aτ(p,ω)=𝟏{πτ(p,ω)≠⊥}A_{\tau}(p,\omega)=\mathbf{1}\{\pi_{\tau}(p,\omega)\neq\bot\}, where AτA_{\tau} indicates whether the policy releases an output. The goal is to control the target loss among released outputs at level α\alpha with confidence 1−δ1-\delta, where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is the risk budget and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) is the calibration failure probability. A fixed candidate stream is the important special case ω=𝐘=Y1:N\omega=\mathbf{Y}=Y_{1:N} with Yk∼G(⋅∣p)Y_{k}\sim G(\cdot\mid p), where NN is the maximum budget and k∈[N]k\in[N] indexes candidates.

SHIP aligns the calibration unit with the release policy. Each exchangeable observation is a held-out prompt together with a complete policy rollout, rather than one candidate pooled across prompts. As illustrated in Figure 2, SHIP evaluates the exact release rule and returns the most permissive threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star} whose policy-level risk bound satisfies α\alpha. Threshold-independent streams support counterfactual replay of many thresholds from one cache. History-dependent procedures are instead evaluated from complete trajectories generated by the deployed adaptive policy. This distinction changes computational reuse, not the released-output estimand.

3.2 Atomic Prompt Verification

To localize compositional failures, we represent each prompt by 𝒜⁡(p)={aj​(p)}j=1mp\mathcal{A}(p)=\{a_{j}(p)\}_{j=1}^{m_{p}}, where aj​(p)a_{j}(p) is the jj-th atomic requirement and mp=|𝒜⁡(p)|m_{p}=|\mathcal{A}(p)|. The atoms cover existence, count, attribute binding, spatial relation, and action. Each atom becomes a yes/no question following TIFA and DSG (21; 12).

For a candidate YY, the continuous atom score is:

qj(v)​(Y,p)=PrVv⁡(“Yes”∣Y,aj​(p)),v∈{sel,tgt},q_{j}^{(v)}(Y,p)=\Pr_{V_{v}}\!\left(\text{``Yes''}\mid Y,a_{j}(p)\right),\qquad v\in\{\mathrm{sel},\mathrm{tgt}\}, (1)

where VselV_{\mathrm{sel}} is the selector VLM available at deployment, VtgtV_{\mathrm{tgt}} is an independent target VLM used only offline, and qj(v)​(Y,p)∈[0,1]q_{j}^{(v)}(Y,p)\in[0,1] is the next-token probability that judge VvV_{v} assigns to a positive answer. Continuous probabilities avoid the brittleness of hard yes/no decoding (30).

We aggregate atom scores using Soft-TIFA geometric-mean (Soft-TIFA-GM) risk:

s⁡(Y,p)\displaystyle s(Y,p) =1−(∏j=1mpqj(sel)​(Y,p))1/mp,\displaystyle=1-\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m_{p}}q_{j}^{(\mathrm{sel})}(Y,p)\right)^{1/m_{p}}, (2)
ℓ⁡(Y,p)\displaystyle\ell(Y,p) =1−(∏j=1mpqj(tgt)​(Y,p))1/mp,\displaystyle=1-\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m_{p}}q_{j}^{(\mathrm{tgt})}(Y,p)\right)^{1/m_{p}},

where s⁡(Y,p)s(Y,p) is the online selector risk and ℓ⁡(Y,p)\ell(Y,p) is the held-out target loss. The geometric mean penalizes a low atom score multiplicatively, which is appropriate when one violated requirement can invalidate prompt following. We use Qwen2.5-VL (5) for VselV_{\mathrm{sel}} and Qwen3-VL (4) for VtgtV_{\mathrm{tgt}}. InternVL3 provides an alternative-architecture robustness check (11; 47). Because the policy never observes ℓ\ell, calibration measures held-out risk rather than the selector’s self-score.

3.3 Candidate-to-Policy Calibration Mismatch

Candidate-level calibration and deployment control different random variables:

Rimg​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{img}}(\tau) =𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Y,p)∣s⁡(Y,p)≤τ],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell(Y,p)\mid s(Y,p)\leq\tau\right], (3)
Rπ​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\pi}(\tau) =𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(πτ​(p,ω),p)∣Aτ​(p,ω)=1],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell\!\left(\pi_{\tau}(p,\omega),p\right)\mid A_{\tau}(p,\omega)=1\right],
Cπ​(τ)\displaystyle C_{\pi}(\tau) =Pr[Aτ(p,ω)=1],\displaystyle=\Pr\!\left[A_{\tau}(p,\omega)=1\right],

where Y∼G(⋅∣p)Y\sim G(\cdot\mid p) is one candidate, Rimg​(τ)R_{\mathrm{img}}(\tau) is candidate risk conditional on passing, Rπ​(τ)R_{\pi}(\tau) is released-output risk, and Cπ​(τ)C_{\pi}(\tau) is coverage. Accept/reject evaluates only Y1Y_{1}. Best-of-NN with rejection releases the minimum-risk candidate if it passes. Sequential stopping releases the first passing candidate. Adaptive policies may alter later candidates using earlier verifier feedback. The same threshold can therefore induce different released distributions across policies.

For a prompt pp, let qτ​(p)=Pr⁡[s⁡(Y,p)≤τ∣p]q_{\tau}(p)=\Pr[s(Y,p)\leq\tau\mid p] and rimg,τ(p)=𝔼[ℓ(Y,p)∣s(Y,p)≤τ,p]r_{\mathrm{img},\tau}(p)=\mathbb{E}[\ell(Y,p)\mid s(Y,p)\leq\tau,p], where these terms are the candidate pass probability and conditional loss. Likewise, let aπ,τ​(p)=Pr⁡[Aτ​(p,ω)=1∣p]a_{\pi,\tau}(p)=\Pr[A_{\tau}(p,\omega)=1\mid p] and rπ,τ(p)=𝔼[ℓ(πτ(p,ω),p)∣Aτ(p,ω)=1,p]r_{\pi,\tau}(p)=\mathbb{E}[\ell(\pi_{\tau}(p,\omega),p)\mid A_{\tau}(p,\omega)=1,p], where these terms are the policy acceptance probability and released-output loss.

Proposition 1 (Candidate calibration is not policy calibration). Conditioning on the prompt gives:

Rimg​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{img}}(\tau) =𝔼p​[qτ​(p)​rimg,τ​(p)]𝔼p​[qτ​(p)],\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p}[q_{\tau}(p)r_{\mathrm{img},\tau}(p)]}{\mathbb{E}_{p}[q_{\tau}(p)]}, (4)
Rπ​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\pi}(\tau) =𝔼p​[aπ,τ​(p)​rπ,τ​(p)]𝔼p​[aπ,τ​(p)],\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p}[a_{\pi,\tau}(p)r_{\pi,\tau}(p)]}{\mathbb{E}_{p}[a_{\pi,\tau}(p)]},

where 𝔼p\mathbb{E}_{p} denotes expectation over deployment prompts. Consequently, Rimg​(τ)≤αR_{\mathrm{img}}(\tau)\leq\alpha does not imply Rπ​(τ)≤αR_{\pi}(\tau)\leq\alpha. Selection changes the prompt weights from qτq_{\tau} to aπ,τa_{\pi,\tau} and the conditional loss from rimg,τr_{\mathrm{img},\tau} to rπ,τr_{\pi,\tau}. The latter term incorporates extreme-score selection, first-hit stopping, tournament outcomes, and history-dependent refinement.

3.4 Policy-Level Calibration and Validity

SHIP evaluates the policy on 𝒫cal={pi}i=1M\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{p_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}, where MM is the number of held-out calibration prompts. For each τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, it executes or exactly replays the policy with randomness ωi,τ\omega_{i,\tau} and sets Ai​(τ)=Aτ​(pi,ωi,τ)A_{i}(\tau)=A_{\tau}(p_{i},\omega_{i,\tau}). When Ai​(τ)=1A_{i}(\tau)=1, it records Li​(τ)=ℓ⁡(πτ​(pi,ωi,τ),pi)L_{i}(\tau)=\ell(\pi_{\tau}(p_{i},\omega_{i,\tau}),p_{i}), where Li​(τ)∈[0,1]L_{i}(\tau)\in[0,1] is the loss of the released output. Replayable policies may share a cached trajectory across thresholds. History-dependent policies use complete rollouts that preserve their native state transitions. Then:

nτ\displaystyle n_{\tau} =∑i=1MAi​(τ),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{M}A_{i}(\tau), (5)
R^π​(τ)\displaystyle\widehat{R}_{\pi}(\tau) =1nτ∑i:Ai​(τ)=1Li(τ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{\tau}}\sum_{i:A_{i}(\tau)=1}L_{i}(\tau),

where nτn_{\tau} is the accepted calibration count and R^π​(τ)\widehat{R}_{\pi}(\tau) is the empirical policy risk for nτ>0n_{\tau}>0.

SHIP computes:

Uδ′​(τ)\displaystyle U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau) =R^π​(τ)+log⁡(1/δ′)2​nτ,\displaystyle=\widehat{R}_{\pi}(\tau)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta^{\prime})}{2n_{\tau}}}, (6)
τ⋆\displaystyle\tau^{\star} =max⁡{τ∈𝒯:Uδ′​(τ)≤α},\displaystyle=\max\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}:U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau)\leq\alpha\},

where δ′∈(0,1)\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1) is the failure level assigned to one threshold, Uδ′​(τ)U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau) is the Hoeffding upper bound, and τ⋆\tau^{\star} is the most permissive feasible threshold. We set Uδ′​(τ)=+∞U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau)=+\infty for nτ=0n_{\tau}=0 and return ⊥\bot if none is feasible.

For finite-sample certification, SHIP fixes 𝒯\mathcal{T} before calibration and sets δ′=δ/|𝒯|\delta^{\prime}=\delta/|\mathcal{T}|, where |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| is the number of thresholds. This Bonferroni allocation makes all threshold bounds simultaneously valid and is a standard Learn-then-Test procedure (1; 7). The confidence construction is not our methodological claim. Our contribution is to apply valid threshold selection to the losses produced by complete policy replay. Sharper selective-risk certificates (6; 45) can replace the Hoeffding bound without changing the policy-level estimand.

Certification is inexpensive when one threshold-independent stream can be replayed. If a threshold changes the state transitions of a history-dependent policy, exact evaluation may instead require a complete rollout for every prompt and threshold, giving naive offline cost proportional to M​|𝒯|M|\mathcal{T}|. We therefore report formal fixed-grid certification for replayable streams and treat the adaptive-policy operating points as descriptive. Reducing valid calibration cost for threshold-dependent search remains an open problem.

Proposition 2 (Finite-sample validity). Assume the calibration prompts and their complete policy rollouts are independent and identically distributed draws from the deployment procedure, and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be fixed independently of them. With δ′=δ/|𝒯|\delta^{\prime}=\delta/|\mathcal{T}|, any threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star} returned by (6) satisfies:

Pr[Rπ(τ⋆)≤α]≥1−δ,\Pr\!\left[R_{\pi}(\tau^{\star})\leq\alpha\right]\geq 1-\delta, (7)

where the probability is over the calibration prompts and policy randomness.

A proof is provided in the Supplementary Material.

3.5 Sequential Calibrated Stopping

Let Kτ​(p,𝐘)=min⁡({k∈[N]:s⁡(Yk,p)≤τ}∪{+∞})K_{\tau}(p,\mathbf{Y})=\min(\{k\in[N]:s(Y_{k},p)\leq\tau\}\cup\{+\infty\}), where KτK_{\tau} is the first passing index and equals +∞+\infty if none passes. The sequential policy is:

πτseq​(p,𝐘)\displaystyle\pi_{\tau}^{\mathrm{seq}}(p,\mathbf{Y}) ={YKτ​(p,𝐘),Kτ​(p,𝐘)≤N,⊥,Kτ​(p,𝐘)>N,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}Y_{K_{\tau}(p,\mathbf{Y})},&K_{\tau}(p,\mathbf{Y})\leq N,\\ \bot,&K_{\tau}(p,\mathbf{Y})>N,\end{cases} (8)
Aτseq​(p,𝐘)\displaystyle A_{\tau}^{\mathrm{seq}}(p,\mathbf{Y}) ={Kτ(p,𝐘)≤N},\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{K_{\tau}(p,\mathbf{Y})\leq N\right\},

where πτseq\pi_{\tau}^{\mathrm{seq}} releases the first passing candidate and AτseqA_{\tau}^{\mathrm{seq}} indicates whether one exists within budget. Easy prompts stop early. Difficult prompts use up to NN attempts and otherwise abstain. Calibration evaluates this same first-hit rule, aligning the offline estimand with the online release.

Algorithm 1 summarizes calibration and deployment. For calibration prompt pip_{i}, let ki​(τ)=Kτ​(pi,𝐘i)k_{i}(\tau)=K_{\tau}(p_{i},\mathbf{Y}_{i}), where ki​(τ)k_{i}(\tau) is its first passing index at threshold τ\tau. The threshold grid is fixed before calibration so that the returned threshold inherits Proposition 2.

4 Experiments and Results

4.1 Experimental Protocol

Models and Benchmarks.

GenEval2 (24) provides the primary 800800-prompt evaluation. FLUX.1-dev (9) supports the main fixed and adaptive comparisons. Stable Diffusion 3 Medium, SD3.5-Large (16), and SDXL (33) test backbone transfer. FLUX.1-Kontext-dev (8) supports image editing. GenAI-Bench (28), T2I-CompBench (22), DSG-1k (12), and DPG-Bench (20) test prompt-distribution transfer. By default, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct provide selector risk and target loss, respectively. InternVL3-8B is the alternative-family target.

Protocol and Metrics.

All primary comparisons use disjoint 400/400400/400 calibration and test prompts, target risk α=0.30\alpha{=}0.30, and calibration failure probability δ=0.10\delta{=}0.10. The main tables report less conservative empirical operating points obtained with pointwise Hoeffding bounds. We call an operating point calibration-feasible when its calibration UCB does not exceed α\alpha. This empirical designation does not inherit Proposition 2 because pointwise bounds do not account for threshold search. The finite-sample certification study applies Algorithm 1 with the prespecified grid 𝒯={0,0.005,…,1}\mathcal{T}=\{0,0.005,\ldots,1\} and |𝒯|=201|\mathcal{T}|=201. Coverage is the fraction of prompts receiving an output. Released-output risk is mean held-out target loss conditioned on release. Compute is reported as full-generation equivalents, total online VLM calls, and wall-clock time. Prompt bootstrap intervals preserve complete policy trajectories.

Comparisons.

Fixed-search comparisons include random release, best-of-NN rejection, and sequential first-pass release. Adaptive policies include the Flash-BoN VLM tournament (35), RAISE refinement (23), history-dependent prompt rewriting, ProbeSelect early trajectory selection (19), and ADE-CoT image editing (34). The pooled-candidate heuristic fits a threshold after treating all completed candidates as observations, although candidates from the same prompt are dependent. It is included as a common descriptive practice rather than a prompt-level certificate. A one-candidate-per-prompt sensitivity removes this pseudoreplication. SHIP instead fits the threshold to outputs of the complete policy under the same split, selector, and target judge. The Supplementary Document reports the prompt-unit sensitivity and compares our adaptive-policy reproductions with their original metrics.

4.2 Candidate-to-Policy Mismatch across Search Policies

Sequential Search Exposes the Estimand Shift.

Figure 3a isolates the effect on a fixed FLUX candidate stream. The naive pooled threshold gives sequential released risks of 0.2340.234, 0.2780.278, and 0.3100.310 as NN grows from 44 to 1616. At N=16N{=}16, the interval [0.267,0.355][0.267,0.355] overlaps the target, so the crossing is not statistically resolved. Pooling also confounds the estimand shift with within-prompt dependence: one-candidate-per-prompt calibration gives risk 0.1960.196, versus 0.1620.162 for policy calibration. Thus the magnitude is design-sensitive, but the candidate and policy objectives remain distinct. The Supplementary Document gives prompt-unit and independent-stream analyses plus a controlled example approaching gap 1−α1-\alpha.

The Mismatch Generalizes beyond Fixed Search.

Table 1 applies the same descriptive protocol to four FLUX policies. Naive pooled thresholds produce pointwise UCBs from 0.3550.355 to 0.4720.472. Sequential first-pass release, Flash-BoN, and history-dependent rewriting have test risks of 0.3100.310, 0.3610.361, and 0.3280.328, respectively. RAISE has a lower test point estimate of 0.2440.244, although its calibration UCB is 0.3550.355. These rows diagnose how a pooled threshold behaves after deployment search. They do not constitute a valid prompt-level candidate certificate.

SHIP reduces every descriptive policy-level UCB to at most 0.2990.299, with test risk at most 0.2080.208. Search design sets the attainable coverage and cost profile, while policy-level calibration determines which outputs may be released, as illustrated in Figure 4.

4.3 Risk, Coverage, and Compute Tradeoffs

Coverage Is a Tunable Operating Characteristic.

Figure 3c sweeps α\alpha rather than selecting a favorable threshold. Coverage rises from 0.2530.253 to 0.5570.557 as α\alpha increases from 0.200.20 to 0.500.50, while risk tracks the requested budget. Best-of-44 rejection covers more prompts but always uses four generations. Lower coverage at a strict budget therefore reflects deliberate abstention.

Search Policy Determines the Efficiency Profile.

At risk 0.1660.166, Figure 5 shows that Flash-BoN is fastest, RAISE has the highest coverage, and rewriting uses the fewest VLM calls. Sequential SHIP is intermediate, and no policy is best under every cost measure.

4.4 Robustness and Generalization

Adaptive Policies Transfer across Backbones and Tasks.

On SD3.5-Large, ProbeSelect with SHIP reaches risk 0.1960.196, UCB 0.2980.298, and coverage 0.4280.428 using 1.801.80 rather than 5.005.00 full-denoise equivalents. On FLUX.1-Kontext-dev, ADE-CoT with SHIP reaches edit loss 0.1710.171 and UCB 0.2980.298, while candidate calibration is infeasible. These results support calibration transfer, not lower native editing cost. Complete operating points appear in the Supplementary Document.

Additional Robustness Checks.

Sequential SHIP remains below target across backbones, but SDXL coverage falls to 0.1130.113 and SD3 transfer requires recalibration at risk 0.3030.303. At N=16N{=}16, the certificate shows no target crossing across 200200 cached-stream splits with mean risk 0.1480.148 and coverage 0.3910.391. These splits reuse generations and omit rerun variability. Full results are supplementary.

Human Released-Output Audit.

Human atomic loss falls from 0.1120.112 to 0.0760.076 and strict any-failure from 0.3800.380 to 0.2800.280 (Table 2). Because calibration uses machine loss, this corroborates improvement but is not a human-risk certificate. The Supplementary Document reports the audit protocol, aggregation definitions, and aggregate agreement statistics.

4.5 Evaluator and Failure Analysis

Why Fine-Grained Risk Matters.

Soft-TIFA-GM gives Spearman 0.9280.928, AUROC 0.9750.975, and the lowest non-oracle risk. Scalar rewards yield no feasible set, so ranking alone is insufficient.

Residual Failures.

Failures concentrate in counting, spatial, and action. Prompts with 99 to 1010 atoms reach risk 0.3980.398 at 0.050.05 coverage, showing that average control does not ensure subgroup service.

5 Conclusion

Verifier-guided generation releases a policy-selected output rather than an independent candidate. SHIP calibrates this deployed object by replaying the policy on held-out prompts and bounding released-image loss. Across fixed and adaptive search, policy-level calibration better characterized released-output risk than pooled-candidate thresholds and recovered feasible risk, coverage, and compute tradeoffs. Search determines the attainable quality, coverage, and cost frontier, while calibration determines which operating points may be released.

Validity requires a prespecified grid, exchangeability, bounded loss, and faithful replay. Threshold-dependent adaptive search remains descriptive because exact calibration may require a rollout per prompt and threshold. A held-out VLM defines loss, making the human audit corroborative rather than a human-risk certificate. SHIP controls average rather than subgroup risk. Evaluator drift, hard-prompt abstention, and distribution shift remain boundaries.

Future work should develop sharper bounds, group-aware objectives, and shift detection. More broadly, reliability should be calibrated on the complete deployed decision process that releases an output, not on upstream candidates.

Supplementary Material

Overview

This document expands the evidence behind the main paper without changing its evaluation protocol or reported operating points. Section A specifies the generation, verification, calibration, and uncertainty procedures. Section B states the formal scope of SHIP and proves Proposition 2. Section C diagnoses the candidate-to-policy mismatch through mechanism, calibration-unit and independent-stream analyses. Section D gives the adaptive-policy results and Section E tests robustness. Sections F to I provide qualitative, fixed-search, human, and evaluator evidence. Section J states the remaining deployment boundaries. Unless stated otherwise, experiments use GenEval2 with FLUX.1-dev, Qwen2.5-VL Soft-TIFA-GM selector risk, Qwen3-VL Soft-TIFA-GM target loss, α=0.30\alpha{=}0.30, δ=0.10\delta{=}0.10, and disjoint sets of 400400 calibration prompts and 400400 test prompts.

A Evaluation Protocol and Implementation Details

Generation and verification.

FLUX.1-dev uses 2828 denoising steps, guidance 3.53.5, and 1024×10241024\times 1024 resolution. SD3 Medium uses 2828 steps and classifier-free guidance 7.07.0. SDXL uses 3030 steps and guidance 7.07.0 at the same resolution. Candidate index kk corresponds to generation seed k−1k-1. The selector checkpoint is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and the primary target is Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. InternVL3-8B supplies the alternative-family target. Atom questions and expected answers are frozen in the GenEval2 metadata. Each query appends “Answer in one word.” The evaluator sums the next-token probabilities of valid capitalization, whitespace, and numeric variants before geometric-mean aggregation.

Calibration units and statistical summaries.

One prompt and its complete policy trajectory form one exchangeable unit for SHIP. The pooled-candidate heuristic instead treats completed images as observations even when several images share a prompt. We label this heuristic naive and empirical throughout. The one-candidate-per-prompt sensitivity restores the prompt as the sampling unit, but its pointwise threshold scan is not a simultaneous certificate. Test intervals use prompt bootstrap resampling of complete release or abstention outcomes. Human-policy differences use the same prompt-level paired resampling. Zero coverage denotes an infeasible operating point and is never interpreted as zero deployment risk. Unless a table states otherwise, each fixed-stream operating point is computed once on the frozen candidate stream and each interval uses 50005000 prompt-level bootstrap replicates with a fixed analysis seed. Candidate-stream replications and cached-stream split studies state their seed ranges and repetition counts separately. Bootstrap resampling quantifies prompt-sampling uncertainty and is not counted as an independent generation run.

Hardware.

Core generation and scoring runs use one NVIDIA RTX 5090 with 32 GB memory, driver 580.159.03, CUDA 12.8, and PyTorch 2.10.0. Baseline-specific environments use the package versions required by their official implementations. Reported seconds are single-GPU wall-clock measurements.

Adaptive-Policy Implementations.

Flash-BoN uses its full VLM tournament over inexpensive drafts. RAISE uses its analyzer, rewriter, verifier, generation, and editing actions. The history-dependent rewriting ablation retains failure-conditioned prompt rewriting and generation while disabling image editing. ProbeSelect launches five SD3.5-Large trajectories and retains one after the probe at 20%20\% of denoising. It uses 2828 steps and classifier-free guidance 7.07.0. ADE-CoT follows its official N=32N{=}32 editing protocol. Every completed candidate and released output in the common comparison is rescored by the same selector and target judge. Reported VLM calls include search-native verification and the release gate.

B Formal Scope and Finite-Sample Validity

Proof of Proposition 2.

For any fixed τ\tau and nτ>0n_{\tau}>0, the accepted losses are bounded in [0,1][0,1]. Hoeffding’s inequality therefore gives Pr[Rπ(τ)>Uδ′(τ)]≤δ′\Pr[R_{\pi}(\tau)>U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau)]\leq\delta^{\prime}. A union bound over the |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| prespecified thresholds makes every bound valid simultaneously with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. On this event, the selected threshold obeys Rπ​(τ⋆)≤Uδ′​(τ⋆)≤αR_{\pi}(\tau^{\star})\leq U_{\delta^{\prime}}(\tau^{\star})\leq\alpha. □\square

Table 3 separates the statistical tool from the paper’s application-level contribution. Learn-then-Test supplies simultaneous parameter selection. SHIP defines the calibrated observation as the output of the complete T2I release policy. SCOPE-Gen and SAFER control set-valued or filtered generation objects. BOKBO controls an execute-or-abstain decision for verifier-best actions. These objects are related, but none makes a candidate-level threshold automatically valid after a different search and stopping policy is composed with it.

C Diagnosing the Candidate-to-Policy Mismatch

Mechanism decomposition.

Table 4 implements the decomposition in Proposition 1. For sequential release at N=16N{=}16, changing candidate pass weights to policy acceptance weights contributes +0.108+0.108 to risk. Prompt bootstrap gives an interval from 0.0830.083 to 0.1330.133. Replacing the mean passing-candidate loss by the first released candidate contributes −0.009-0.009, with an interval from −0.035-0.035 to 0.0170.017. The observed sequential mismatch is therefore dominated by prompt reweighting in this experiment. Best-of-NN selection has a more negative within-prompt component, which offsets part of the same reweighting.

Sensitivity to the candidate calibration unit.

The pooled heuristic combines 1616 correlated candidates from each prompt and thus reports 64006400 calibration observations. Table 5 compares it with two prompt-level alternatives and direct policy replay on the same fixed N=16N{=}16 stream. The pooled sequential row reproduces the risk 0.3100.310 in the main paper. Choosing one fixed candidate per prompt reduces the point estimate to 0.1960.196, so the numerical budget crossing depends on the candidate calibration design. Direct policy replay targets the deployed first-pass output and gives risk 0.1620.162. The comparison supports an estimand distinction, not a claim that every candidate-level construction must cross α\alpha on every finite dataset.

Independent candidate-stream replication.

To test dependence on generation randomness, we repeat the N=16N{=}16 comparison on two nonoverlapping seed streams over the same frozen subset of 9696 calibration and 104104 test prompts. Table 6 shows the same ordering in both streams. The smaller subset produces wider intervals, so this is replication evidence rather than a replacement for the full 800800-prompt experiment.

Representative release decisions.

Figure 6 shows two real prompt-level candidate streams with different relation failures. In each case, the policy rejects an early high-risk image and releases a later candidate that satisfies the stated relation. The examples visualize the released object evaluated by SHIP rather than serving as additional quantitative evidence.

D Adaptive Search and Editing Policies

The adaptive results distinguish search quality from release calibration. Table 7 shows that the policies occupy different points on the same matched-risk frontier. Tables 8 and 9 then test early trajectory selection and iterative image editing. SHIP changes which completed policy outcomes are released. It does not claim the native search contributions or their internal compute savings.

E Robustness across Models, Data, Judges, and Splits

Prompt-distribution transfer.

Table 10 expands the middle panel of Figure 7. The release threshold τ=0.322\tau{=}0.322 is fit on GenEval2 seed-00 calibration images and transferred unchanged to the seed-00 FLUX images for each prompt set. Transfer remains below the nominal budget in these four cases, but the coverage and risk shifts show why the result should not be interpreted as a distribution-shift guarantee.

Alternative target judge.

Table 11 replaces the Qwen3 target with InternVL3 while keeping the Qwen2.5 selector fixed. The selector correlates strongly with both targets, and policy-level calibration preserves the ordering of accept or reject, best-of-44, and sequential policies. Absolute risks change, which reinforces the interpretation that the target judge defines the measured loss.

Pointwise operating points and fixed-grid certification.

Table 12 separates the practical pointwise scan used in the main result tables from the prespecified-grid procedure in Proposition 2. Both rows use one prompt trajectory as one observation and average over 200200 cached-stream splits at N=16N{=}16. The fixed-grid row has no empirical target crossing and is the only row in this comparison with simultaneous finite-sample validity. The pointwise row attains higher mean coverage but is reported only as an empirical operating rule.

F Qualitative Evidence from Real Generations

Figure 8 makes the release rule visible at the image level. The candidate streams contain both clear failures and faithful generations for counting, contextual, and structural requirements. The figure is diagnostic rather than a selected success rate. Quantitative evidence is always computed over the complete held-out prompt set.

G Fixed Search, Evaluators, and Failure Diagnostics

Risk and coverage across target budgets.

Table 14 reports every operating point shown on the risk-coverage frontier in the main paper. The threshold is calibrated separately for each target budget. Sequential stopping and best-of-44 rejection use the same candidate bank and target judge. Sequential stopping reduces generation and QA cost because accepted prompts may terminate before the fourth attempt.

Budget sweep.

Table 15 varies the maximum number of candidates at the default risk budget. Coverage rises with NN, while compute grows more slowly than the maximum budget because the sequential policy stops after its first pass.

Cross-Backbone Operating Points.

Table 16 gives the per-backbone numbers summarized in the main text. Held-out risk is below budget for all three generators, while achievable coverage varies substantially.

Where Failures Concentrate.

Table 17 breaks accepted-output quality down by atom type, showing that counting, spatial, and verb atoms are the bottleneck while object existence is nearly solved.

Adaptive-policy generalization.

Tables 7, 8, and 9 provide the complete operating points summarized in the main paper. Table 13 separately checks each reproduction on its native benchmark before applying the shared SHIP evaluation protocol.

H Human Released-Output Audit

The audit evaluates both N=16N{=}16 sequential policies on the same 400400 test prompts. Their released sets contain 267267 distinct images and share 137137 outputs. Blinded views omit policies, thresholds, and machine scores. Two annotators label each atom as yes, no, or uncertain, followed by adjudication of disagreements. Shared outputs are labeled once and reused.

Atomic loss is the fraction of adjudicated atoms not labeled yes. Any-failure marks an image with at least one no or uncertain atom. Intervals resample the full prompt universe while preserving release and abstention. Because machine loss selects the thresholds, Table 18 corroborates the result but does not certify human risk.

I Evaluator Ablations and Modular Cascades

Cheap-to-expensive selector cascades.

The release gate need not score every candidate with the fine-grained evaluator. Table 21 first ranks four candidates with a cheaper holistic score, then sends only the top one or two candidates to the Soft-TIFA-GM gate. Every row uses the same target judge and policy-level release calibration. Sending two candidates improves coverage while using half of the 30.130.1 atom-level QA calls required by scoring all four candidates.

J Controlled Study and Deployment Boundaries

Synthetic controlled study and a lower bound.

To isolate selection from any particular T2I verifier, Figure 9a uses a two-component prompt mixture. A hard prompt occurs with probability 0.50.5 and has candidate failure probability 0.90.9, while an easy prompt has failure probability 0.050.05. The selector score is s=ℓ+εs=\ell+\varepsilon, where ε∼𝒩⁡(0,0.72)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.7^{2}). For every candidate budget, we choose τ\tau so 𝔼⁡[ℓ∣s≤τ]=α\mathbb{E}[\ell\mid s\leq\tau]=\alpha and then deploy best-of-NN or sequential selection. Candidate calibration remains at 0.300.30, yet released risk can exceed the target. Policy calibration stays at or below the target.

Figure 9b studies the limiting construction used below. A prompt is hard with probability ρ\rho. Every hard-prompt candidate has loss 11, every easy-prompt candidate has loss 00, and ε∼𝒩⁡(0,1.52)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1.5^{2}). With N=256N{=}256, released risk reaches 0.640.64 at ρ=0.7\rho{=}0.7 while candidate risk remains 0.300.30.

Proposition 3 (Lower bound on the post-selection gap). In the deterministic-loss mixture of Figure 9b, fix any candidate-level threshold τ\tau with 𝔼⁡[ℓ∣s≤τ]=α\mathbb{E}[\ell\mid s\leq\tau]=\alpha. As N→∞N\to\infty, the best-of-NN released-output risk under τ\tau converges to the hard-prompt share ρ\rho among accepted prompts, while candidate-level risk remains α\alpha. Hence the gap Rπ​(τ)−Rimg​(τ)R_{\pi}(\tau)-R_{\mathrm{img}}(\tau) can be driven to 1−α1-\alpha by increasing ρ\rho. Proof sketch. As N→∞N\to\infty, mink∈[N]⁡s⁡(Yk,p)→−∞\min_{k\in[N]}s(Y_{k},p)\to-\infty, so acceptance approaches one. Hard prompts then release loss 11 and easy prompts release loss 00, giving Rπ​(τ)→ρR_{\pi}(\tau)\to\rho, while the fixed candidate risk remains α\alpha. Taking ρ→1\rho\to 1 yields a gap approaching 1−α1-\alpha. □\square Thus candidate calibration cannot in general be patched into a policy guarantee.

Group-Conditional Risk Control.

A global threshold controls average released risk, not subgroup risk. Table 22 groups prompts by atomicity. The 99 to 1010 atom group has risk 0.3980.398 at 0.050.05 coverage from five releases. Group-SHIP calibrates each group separately and abstains where no threshold is feasible, so it remains a diagnostic rather than a service guarantee.

Per-Deployment Recalibration.

The GenAI-Bench transfer is the tightest case. On SD3, the transferred risk point estimate reaches 0.303>α0.303>\alpha. Table 23 shows that a small deployment-side calibration set returns the average held-out risk below α\alpha, with coverage recovering as ncaln_{\mathrm{cal}} grows.

Sensitivity and Finite-Sample Certification.

The threshold is stable across tested resolutions. Coverage is 0.360.36 at |𝒯|=25|\mathcal{T}|{=}25 and 0.390.39 at full resolution. Calibration sets of 200200 to 400400 prompts yield coverage from 0.360.36 to 0.390.39, with cached-stream crossing rates below δ\delta. Policy recalibration lowers released risk over pooled calibration by 0.0870.087 for FLUX, 0.0960.096 for SD3, and 0.1660.166 for SDXL at N=4N{=}4. One fixed candidate per prompt gives τ=0.322\tau{=}0.322 and, under sequential N=16N{=}16 reuse, risk 0.1960.196 with interval [0.156,0.239][0.156,0.239] at coverage 0.4730.473. Thus the empirical crossing depends on the candidate design, while the population non-implication remains. Empirical-Bernstein did not improve coverage under grid correction. Anytime-valid betting increased coverage but did not reliably remain below δ\delta. Sharper selection-aware concentration remains future work.
